post_title: How many commercial ship crossings of the Strait of Hormuz will be recorded on 12 November 2026?

question.title: How many commercial ship crossings of the Strait of Hormuz will be recorded on 12 November 2026?
question.description:
The Strait of Hormuz — the chokepoint between the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman through which roughly a fifth of global oil and LNG trade passed before the war — has been effectively closed to commercial shipping since 28 February 2026, when the US–Israel–Iran war began. Shipping trackers count 30 October 2026 as day 244–245 of the closure. A Qatar- and Pakistan-brokered memorandum of understanding in June 2026 briefly restored traffic (daily commercial crossings ran at roughly 17–35 during that interlude), but the ceasefire collapsed in July and Iran re-declared the strait closed.

Status quo (as of 30 October 2026): hormuz.now, which counts AIS-visible commercial ships crossing the strait, rates the waterway "Restricted (severely restricted)". Its 7-day average is about 6 commercial crossings per day against a pre-crisis baseline of 84.8 per day (roughly 8% of normal), and recent complete days read 11 crossings on 21 October, 6 on 22 October and 10 on 29 October — day-to-day counts in late October have ranged from about 5 to 12, so single-day figures are noisy. Roughly 470 commercial ships are waiting outside the strait. straits.live, using IMF PortWatch data, separately reports 2 commercial transits on 25 October versus ~85/day pre-crisis (throughput ~2% of normal), war-risk insurance at 32× normal, ~6,000 seafarers stranded, and Brent crude at roughly $112–115/bbl against ~$72 before the war. Tracker methodologies differ substantially — PortWatch-based counts (2–5 transits/day) are far lower than hormuz.now's (6–11/day) — which is why this question pins a single source (hormuz.now) and a single metric (its daily commercial-crossing total).

Diplomacy: on Sunday 25 October 2026 Qatar presented Iran with a draft peace plan whose implementation timetable runs over seven days of daily confidence-building steps, including reopening the Strait of Hormuz and lifting the US blockade of Iranian ports; Tehran was expected to respond by the end of that week (https://www.arabnews.com/middle-east/iran-says-discussing-plan-with-mediators-to-end-war-reopen-hormuz-3008650). Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said on 28 October that Iran is discussing with mediators how to implement the seven-day plan, while Iranian officials have reportedly sought to compress implementation to four days and mediators have discussed an Iran–US meeting in Turkey before 4 November. Analysts frame Iranian incentives around the US midterm elections of 3 November 2026, deep mutual distrust (three US strikes on Iran since June 2025), and Tehran's use of Hormuz as leverage (https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/10/27/irans-calculations-as-us-escalation-looms-trust-midterms-hormuz). A deal implemented in early November would put reopening — and a surge of the vessels now waiting offshore — inside the window of this question, whereas a stalled or collapsed process would leave daily crossings near their current single-digit level.

Resolution data: hormuz.now publishes a per-day archive page for each UTC day (e.g. https://hormuz.now/traffic/2026-10-29) stating that day's total commercial crossings, split into inbound and outbound and by vessel type, with small craft excluded and listed separately, and with IMF PortWatch's own count for the same day shown alongside as a separate series. The same daily series is downloadable from https://hormuz.now/data. Its current counting method has been in use since 19 October 2026.

question.resolution_criteria: This question resolves to hormuz.now's recorded total of commercial ship crossings of the Strait of Hormuz for the UTC day 12 November 2026, as published on the archive page for that day, https://hormuz.now/traffic/2026-11-12, which appears once that UTC day is complete. The resolving value is the whole number the page states as that day's commercial crossings — inbound plus outbound — e.g. a page reading "10 commercial crossings (3 inbound, 7 outbound)" resolves as 10; small-craft crossings, which the page lists separately, are not counted, and the IMF PortWatch transit figure the page displays for the same day (a different series) is ignored. The figure published for that day stands regardless of the AIS feed coverage hormuz.now reports for it, unless the page explicitly labels the day's count as incomplete or preliminary, in which case resolution waits for that day's finalized figure. If the archive page is unavailable, the row for 2026-11-12 on https://hormuz.now/data is used instead; if no figure for 2026-11-12 is published by 23:59 UTC on 30 November 2026, the question is annulled.
question.fine_print: The figure is read once, at the time of resolution; any later revision by hormuz.now does not change the outcome. If hormuz.now changes its counting methodology before 12 November 2026, the figure it publishes for that day under its then-current method stands.
